justification: The strongest direct evidence is a single human case report with literature review describing seizures in multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome caused by an ACTA2 mutation (PMID 34734057), which constitutes credible but limited evidence rather than replicated causation. Supporting indirect human evidence comes from ACTA2 Arg179 cohorts showing progressive stroke, arterial steno-occlusive disease, and white matter injury (PMID 33199432), all recognized precursors/risk factors for epilepsy, and from ACTA2's role in moyamoya-type cerebrovascular disease (PMIDs 39822761, 28814167). However, no second independent report of ACTA2 variants causing epilepsy per se is present, so "Established" cannot be supported; most remaining articles concern aortic/vascular phenotypes or use ACTA2 merely as a smooth-muscle marker (PMIDs 37320987, 38919852, 32483447), contributing only incidental mentions. Thus "Existing" is the most probable category, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" given the mechanistic (cerebral ischemia → seizures) rather than primary epileptogenic link.

None of the provided articles report genetic variants in CD1C in patients with bipolar disorder, nor any association or linkage study; there is no human genetic evidence at all, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded. The only bipolar-related co-mentions arise because valproic acid and lithium are mood stabilizers used in bipolar disorder; one in vitro human study shows these drugs downregulate group I CD1 (including CD1c) expression during monocyte-derived dendritic cell differentiation (PMID 27639185), and another examines valproate-induced epigenetic changes in murine decidua with no CD1C relevance (PMID 33735658). All remaining papers concern CD1c as a dendritic cell lineage marker in immunology, oncology, infection and histiocytosis, entirely unrelated to psychiatric phenotypes. The pharmacological modulation of CD1 expression offers only a tenuous mechanistic thread, insufficient for a credible biological hypothesis linking CD1C to bipolar pathogenesis, so most weight falls on Novel with some residual probability for Hypothesized.

No article in this set reports ARL13B variants causing or associating with congenital heart disease in patients. The Joubert syndrome case series (PMID 23692786) notes one of 11 patients with congenital heart disease, but the only mutation identified was in CC2D2A, and ARL13B screening yielded no causal variant; this is incidental co-mention rather than evidence. Human ARL13B variant reports (PMID 18674751, 38219074) describe classical Joubert syndrome phenotypes without cardiac involvement. The remaining literature is animal/in vitro work on ciliogenesis, Hedgehog signalling, body-axis/left–right patterning and ciliopathy mechanisms (PMID 27682584, 26582389, 27153923, 32169553), which provides a plausible biological rationale (cilia/Shh-dependent cardiac and laterality development) but no phenotype data in heart, supporting at most a Hypothesized relationship.

Only one article (PMID 41863516) connects C10orf90 to Alzheimer's disease: a multi-omics study integrating AD GWAS summary statistics with single-cell transcriptomics (scPagwas) plus machine-learning selection, which nominated C10orf90 as a key glial-associated candidate gene expressed in oligodendrocytes and astrocytes. This is human data with a genetic-risk-informed component, but C10orf90 itself was selected largely by expression-based machine learning and diagnostic modeling rather than by replicated variant-level association in independent probands, so it falls short of "Existing" definitiveness and close to "Hypothesized". No article reports AD-causing variants in C10ORF90 in patients or families, so Established is essentially excluded. The remaining papers concern centrosome/cilium biology (PMID 20844083), tuberculosis resistance (PMID 33661925), 10q26 deletions in developmental phenotypes (PMIDs 27113058, 23495067), and cancer (PMIDs 30672666, 26223354), none of which address Alzheimer's disease; the multigene 10q26 deletions cannot implicate this gene specifically.

None of the provided articles report C10ORF90 sequence variants in patients with congenital heart disease; the clinical reports involve 10q26 terminal deletions associated with short stature, developmental delay or autism, and these contiguous multi-gene deletions cannot implicate C10ORF90 specifically (PMID 27113058, 23495067). Other papers concern unrelated phenotypes (conjunctival melanoma copy number loss, Alzheimer's transcriptomics, tuberculosis resistance GWAS at 10q26.2), representing incidental co-mention rather than cardiac relevance (PMIDs 30672666, 41863516, 33661925). The only biologically suggestive item is the centrosomal/ciliary function study showing C10ORF90 contains an ALMS motif, localizes to centrosomes, and is required for primary cilium assembly (PMID 20844083); since ciliary dysfunction is a well-recognized mechanism in heart development and laterality defects, this provides a thin, indirect hypothesized basis, though the work is in cultured cells and makes no cardiac claim. Overall the evidence base is dominated by incidental co-mentions, so Novel is most likely, with modest weight for Hypothesized.

Nearly all retrieved articles use "CHD" to mean coronary heart disease (network pharmacology/molecular docking studies) or concern asthma/COPD/hypertension pharmacogenetics, which are homonym or off-target contexts and do not support a congenital heart disease link. No human study reports ADRB2 variants in congenital heart disease probands or families; the mouse mutation-mapping paper (PMID 24306492) identified Dnaic1, not ADRB2. The strongest relevant evidence is the zebrafish fenbuconazole study (PMID 38588970), where decreased ADRB2 protein accompanied multigenerational cardiac developmental defects and downregulated cardiac developmental genes, explicitly framed as insight into congenital heart disease — this is animal/functional data, supporting Hypothesized rather than Existing. A single human cardiomyopathy exome case with a disruptive ADRB2 variant (PMID 25979592) concerns dilated cardiomyopathy, not congenital heart disease, and is an isolated variant of unknown significance. Therefore points concentrate on Hypothesized, with substantial residual probability for Novel given the incidental nature of most co-mentions.

The bulk of the evidence is mechanistic and non-human: β2-adrenergic signaling modulates Aβ production in SH-SY5Y cells (28476886), Adrb2 mediates Aβ-induced wakefulness in zebrafish (32660691), conditional microglial adrb2 deletion alters neuroinflammation in 5XFAD mice (39696597), and ADRB2 activation rescues mitophagy/tau pathology and exercise-induced autophagy benefits in APP/PS1 mice (36208707, 37964627, 41668187). These establish a biologically plausible, pathway-level link but contain no human genetic association data for AD risk. The only human-variant item is a pharmacogenetics review listing ADRB2 among pharmagenes affecting treatment response for anxiety/depression in AD patients (36628952), which is drug-response background rather than primary evidence of variant-driven AD risk; other ADRB2 mentions (asthma pharmacogenetics, cardiomyopathy panel, multiplexed assays) are unrelated to AD. No article reports causal ADRB2 variants in independent AD probands or families, so Established is effectively excluded, and Novel is implausible given the strong functional rationale.

No article reports ARL13B variants in Alzheimer's disease patients or any human genetic association with AD; all human genetic evidence links ARL13B to Joubert syndrome and related ciliopathies (PMID 18674751, 30269812), so Established and Existing are excluded. The only AD-relevant paper (PMID 28931427) studies 5-HT6 receptor regulation of primary cilia function and cognition in a mouse AD model, where ARL13B typically serves as a cilia marker — this provides a weak, animal-based biological rationale rather than genetic evidence. A possible secondary mechanistic thread is the ARL13B–ARL3 cascade in stress-induced cellular senescence (PMID 37019904), relevant to aging biology but not specific to AD. The remaining literature concerns ciliogenesis, retinal/photoreceptor development, neuronal migration, and ciliary transition zone assembly, which are mechanistically interesting for neurodevelopment but not for AD pathogenesis. Points are therefore split between Hypothesized (ciliary signaling in cognition in an AD mouse model) and Novel (essentially incidental co-mention).

ACTA2 Arg179 (R189H/R179H) de novo heterozygous variants cause multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, whose cardinal feature is a large persistent ductus arteriosus, a bona fide congenital heart defect; PMID 28328125 reports two independent probands with this variant plus aortopulmonary window, coarctation and interrupted aortic arch, and PMID 34734057 is an additional independent MSMDS patient with cardiac involvement. PMID 41643506 adds a family in which carriers of a novel ACTA2 indel had congenital heart disease plus fatal aortic dissection, and PMID 33199432 describes a 27-patient Arg179 cohort, supporting replication in humans. Several other papers (28814167, 32599028, 28659821) cite ACTA2 in relation to PDA/BAV-type cardiovascular malformations as background rather than primary evidence. Weight is placed mainly on Established, with meaningful residual probability on Existing because the direct CHD-focused human reports here are small case reports rather than large independent cohort-based causal studies.

Nearly all retrieved articles concern CAPN3 as the cause of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD2A/LGMDR1) and autosomal dominant calpainopathy (PMIDs 28881388, 32896923, 32342993, 21496626, 9150160, 30919934), with no Alzheimer's disease content. Alzheimer's is mentioned only incidentally in calpain family reviews (PMIDs 11516996, 12843569), where the AD link is attributed to calpain-1/calpain-2 overactivation, not CAPN3, making these co-mentions rather than evidence. The only AD-specific article is a human fusiform gyrus epigenetic study (PMID 32854783), whose abstract does not implicate CAPN3 and which concerns methylation/expression rather than causal genetic variants; at best this could provide weak biological (hypothesized-level) support. No study reports CAPN3 variants in AD probands or families, so Established is effectively excluded and Existing is poorly supported. The balance of evidence therefore favors Novel, with some weight to Hypothesized via the general calpain–neurodegeneration biology.

None of the provided articles mention bipolar disorder at all; the ARL13B literature is dominated by primary cilia biology, Joubert syndrome, retinal/photoreceptor degeneration, and kidney cysts. No human genetic study reports ARL13B variants in bipolar patients, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded. A modest weight goes to Hypothesized because ARL13B-dependent ciliary GPCR signaling regulates GABAergic interneuron migration, synaptic connectivity, and excitatory/inhibitory balance in the cortex (PMID 28787594, 23153492), mechanisms broadly implicated in psychiatric disorders — but these are mouse studies and are not linked to bipolar disorder specifically. Overall, the co-mention is incidental and the evidence base best supports a Novel classification.

None of the provided articles examine schizophrenia at all; the phenotypes covered are 10q26 terminal deletion with short stature (without intellectual disability or behavioral problems), Alzheimer's disease glial transcriptomics, centrosome/cilium biology, tuberculosis infection resistance, and breast cancer risk. No study reports C10orf90 variants in schizophrenia probands or families, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. A weak basis for Hypothesized exists because C10orf90 lies in a neurodevelopmentally implicated 10q26 region (co-deleted with DOCK1/CALY, candidate intellectual-disability genes) and was flagged as a glia-associated gene in an AD multi-omics analysis, offering loose brain-relevant biology. However, these are incidental co-mentions with no logical link to schizophrenia, so Novel receives the bulk of the probability.

None of the supplied articles mention autism, autism spectrum disorder, or any neurodevelopmental/behavioral phenotype attributable to ACTA2 variants. The literature is uniformly focused on ACTA2 in thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection, multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, moyamoya/cerebrovascular occlusive disease, and vascular smooth muscle biology (PMIDs 33199432, 39822761, 26837258, 30242502). The only tangential neurological relevance is cerebrovascular stroke and white matter injury in ACTA2 Arg179 patients, which is a vascular rather than a recognized autism precursor mechanism, giving a weak basis for a "hypothesized" brain-related link. No human genetic study here reports ACTA2 variants in autism probands or families, so Established is effectively excluded and Existing is very unlikely.

None of the provided articles mention Autism Spectrum Disorder in any form. All papers concern CD1C as a marker of dendritic cell biology, lipid antigen presentation, histiocytosis, myeloid neoplasia, asthma, lupus, COVID-19, and tumor microenvironments. There are no genetic variant studies, no neurodevelopmental phenotypes, and no plausible mechanistic link to autism presented in this corpus. The only genetic study (PMID 10395104) examines CD1 polymorphisms across ethnic groups without any disease-phenotype association, let alone autism. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

Two human reports directly link CAPN3 variation to epilepsy: a family in which heterozygous CAPN3 mutation carriers had genetic generalised epilepsy while a homozygote had LGMD (PMID 31011535), and a single case of LGMD2A with idiopathic generalised epilepsy whose authors themselves question whether this is coincidence (PMID 16816913). A further case reports epilepsy with multiple heterozygous variants including CAPN3, but the de novo KCNC1 variant is the far more plausible driver (PMID 35299674), and a review merely restates the purported CAPN3–epilepsy link as background (PMID 34549305). The overwhelming majority of the remaining literature concerns CAPN3 in limb-girdle muscular dystrophy with no epilepsy phenotype, so replication in independent, well-powered cohorts is lacking. This fits "Existing" (credible but limited/anecdotal human evidence) rather than "Established"; a small probability remains for Hypothesized if the two case-level reports are judged coincidental co-occurrence.

Only one article in the list mentions schizophrenia at all (PMID 38612385), and it explicitly reports that the CD1c/CD2 exosome epitope pattern distinguished late-onset Alzheimer's disease but NOT schizophrenia from healthy controls — a negative result for CD1C in SCZ. All remaining papers concern CD1c as a dendritic cell/monocyte lineage marker in immunology, oncology, infection, dermatology, or lipid antigen presentation, with no relevance to schizophrenia pathophysiology. No genetic variant studies, no probands or families, and no expression/pathway data linking CD1C to psychosis are present. Therefore no basis exists for Established or Existing; the small residual Hypothesized weight reflects only the generic neuroimmune/exosome-biomarker framing of PMID 38612385.

None of the provided articles report any genetic or biological link between ACTA2 and schizophrenia. The overwhelming majority concern ACTA2 variants in thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection, smooth muscle contractile vasculopathies, venous malformation, aniridia-like iris anomalies, and glioblastoma CAFs. The only paper mentioning schizophrenia (PMID 37320987) is about DNMT1 overexpression in a mouse ESC line, where Acta2 appears merely as a mesoderm differentiation marker — an incidental co-mention with no relevance to schizophrenia pathogenesis. There are no human genetic association studies, no patient probands, and no mechanistic or expression data connecting ACTA2 to schizophrenia, so the relationship is best classified as Novel.

Every provided article concerns CAPN3 (calpain-3) in the context of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A/LGMDR1, its proteolytic biology, splicing variants, mouse knockouts, and diagnostic gene panels for myopathies. None of the abstracts mention bipolar disorder, psychiatric phenotypes, neuropsychiatric comorbidity, or any CNS pathway plausibly linking calpain-3 to mood disorders; CAPN3 is predominantly skeletal muscle-specific. There are no association studies, case reports, or functional data connecting CAPN3 variants to bipolar disorder in humans or animals. Therefore the gene–phenotype relationship is best classified as Novel, with only trivial probability assigned to a hypothesized link via general calcium-homeostasis or protease biology.

All epilepsy/seizure-related articles in this set use "CD-1" or "CD1" only as the outbred mouse strain designation (e.g., CD-1 mice in neonatal seizure, ketogenic diet, lacosamide, levetiracetam, zonisamide, and pilocarpine studies), which is a homonym and not the CD1C gene. The genuine CD1C papers concern dendritic cell biology, blood DC taxonomy, myeloid neoplasia, histiocytosis, asthma, and lipid antigen presentation, with no mention of seizures or epilepsy. No human genetic variant in CD1C is reported in association with epilepsy, and no biological pathway linking CD1C-mediated lipid antigen presentation to epileptogenesis is proposed in these abstracts. Therefore the gene–phenotype co-mention is incidental and the relationship is best classified as Novel.

None of the provided articles report epilepsy or seizure phenotypes in association with ADGRB2 variants. Human genetic findings implicate ADGRB2 in depressive symptoms (PMID 39472661), neuroticism (PMID 39511343), adult cognitive function (PMID 37231097), schizophrenia candidate variants (PMID 38951484), and a de novo C-terminal mutation causing progressive spastic paraparesis (PMID 28891236) — none of which is a recognized precursor or subtype of epilepsy. Supporting biology (synapse development and plasticity roles of BAI receptors, PMID 26881134; GPCR signaling/proteolytic activation, PMID 20367554; a mouse Bai2 loss-of-function hyperactivity QTL, PMID 28894906) provides only a generic, indirect rationale for neuronal excitability relevance, keeping some weight on Hypothesized. Because no study directly links ADGRB2 variation or function to epileptogenesis, Established cannot be supported and Novel is the most probable category.

No article reports ACTA2 variants causing type 2 diabetes itself; the Mendelian ACTA2 literature concerns smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection, and moyamoya-like cerebrovascular disease (PMIDs 22831780, 33199432, 26837258, 25907466), which are unrelated to T2DM and preclude an "Established" call. The single human genetic study linking ACTA2 to a diabetes-relevant phenotype is PMID 24669260, which found the promoter SNP rs1324551 independently associated with severity of coronary artery stenosis specifically in T2DM patients — a diabetes-related vascular complication rather than T2DM susceptibility, supporting at most "Existing". Biological support comes from α-SMA (ACTA2) as the marker of activated pancreatic/islet stellate cells implicated in islet fibrosis, reduced insulin expression and β-cell apoptosis in T2DM (PMIDs 23500461, 25483957), but these are rat/in vitro studies, placing that evidence in the "Hypothesized" tier. Thus probability mass is split between Existing (one limited human association in diabetic subjects) and Hypothesized (plausible mechanistic/expression link from non-human models), with little weight for Established or Novel.

Multiple human candidate-gene studies report associations of ADRB2 coding variants (Arg16Gly, Gln27Glu) with type 2 diabetes or closely related intermediate traits: an association with T2D risk and age of onset in Taiwanese subjects (PMID 12390345), association of Gln27Glu with elevated NEFA and type 2 diabetes (PMID 11380082), modulation of the age–T2D relationship (PMID 17150099), association with conversion from IGT to T2D in the Finnish DPS (PMID 18249219), and haplotype associations with glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity in obese postmenopausal women (PMID 20829805), plus fasting insulin/HOMA-IR differences by Arg16Gly genotype (PMID 14693408). However, results are inconsistent: a large white cohort of 7,808 subjects (PMID 17221209) and a Korean study (PMID 12077726) found no association, and reviews note the controversial, ethnicity-dependent nature of these findings (PMID 19576569). No study demonstrates a replicated causal role in independent probands or families, so "Established" is not supported; the evidence fits "Existing" (credible but limited/non-definitive human association, including with precursor traits such as insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance).

Only one article in the list connects ACTA2 to bipolar disorder (PMID 28117838), and it reports differential expression of cytoskeletal genes (TPM2, TAGLN, ACTA2) in iPSC-derived cortical neural stem cells from bipolar type I patients versus controls — an expression/functional finding in human-derived cells, not a genetic variant association. No study here reports ACTA2 variants segregating with or associated with bipolar disorder in probands or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is weakly supported at best. All remaining articles concern ACTA2 in thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection, smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, moyamoya-like cerebrovascular disease, venous malformation, and glioblastoma CAFs — phenotypes unrelated to bipolar disorder and representing incidental co-mention. The cerebrovascular/neurodevelopmental biology of ACTA2 plus the human iPSC transcriptomic signal provides a plausible but indirect biological rationale, which best fits the Hypothesized category.

All CAPN3-specific articles concern limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A/R1 (calpainopathy), its mutation spectrum, protein biochemistry, and mouse/iPSC models, with no mention of schizophrenia or any neuropsychiatric phenotype. The schizophrenia-related items (the CNS-2016 meeting abstract compilation and the orexin/prepulse inhibition study) do not involve CAPN3 and are incidental co-mentions within large unrelated abstract collections. There is no human genetic association, no expression/pathway evidence in brain relevant to psychosis, and no animal model linking calpain-3 to schizophrenia-like phenotypes. CAPN3 is predominantly skeletal-muscle expressed, further weakening any biological plausibility argument. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel.

One human genetic association study (PMID 17199132) in 331 AGRE case-parent trios reported an increased risk of autism for the ADRB2 Glu27 homozygous genotype (rs1042714), with modification by pregnancy stress — a credible but single, unreplicated association. A de novo translocation case (PMID 19086034) places a breakpoint near ADRB2, but the breakpoint also implicates SH3TC2, HTR4, and desmocollin genes, so it cannot single out ADRB2 and does not count as causal evidence. Pharmaco-epidemiological studies of prenatal β2-agonist exposure (PMIDs 21874331, 26738885, 33441922) support B2AR overstimulation as a biologically plausible, human-relevant risk mechanism, reinforcing but not proving a genetic causal role. Remaining papers (cardiomyopathy sequencing, pig promoter, mouse FTO/Adrb2, PAGln allostery, multiplexed assays) are not autism-related genetic evidence. Thus the evidence best fits "Existing," with no two independent variant-level causal studies to justify "Established."

Only one article in this set reports human ARL13B variants in patients who actually have epilepsy: PMID 29255182 describes a homozygous missense variant (p.Gly75Arg) in two families with Joubert syndrome whose features include epilepsy, with functional work showing loss of ARL3 GEF activity. PMID 18674751 establishes ARL13B as a Joubert syndrome gene in two families, but epilepsy is not reported as part of their own phenotypic results, so it serves as background for the disease link rather than replication of the seizure phenotype. Other supportive material is non-human or in vitro (Arl13b-mCherry transgenic mice with spontaneous seizures, PMID 32122360; interneuron migration/connectivity and excitation–inhibition balance defects in Arl13b-null mice, PMIDs 28787594, 23153492), which supports a plausible mechanism but cannot substantiate "Established." Several remaining papers mention ARL13B only as a cilia marker or in unrelated gene contexts. Therefore the evidence best fits "Existing," with a mechanistic (hypothesized) underpinning and only a modest chance that it would be judged established.

None of the provided articles mention bipolar disorder in any capacity; the phenotypes discussed include 10q26 terminal deletion syndrome, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, Alzheimer's disease, tuberculosis resistance, conjunctival melanoma, and breast cancer. There are no human genetic association or variant studies linking C10ORF90 to bipolar disorder, so Established and Existing are untenable. A small amount of weight for Hypothesized is warranted because C10orf90 lies in the 10q26 region implicated in neurodevelopmental phenotypes (PMIDs 27113058, 23495067) and has been flagged as a glial/CNS-expressed candidate gene in Alzheimer's multi-omics work (PMID 41863516), plus centrosomal/ciliary functions (PMID 20844083) that are loosely relevant to neurodevelopment. However, these are incidental co-mentions with no bipolar-specific logic, so Novel receives the bulk of the probability.

No article in this list reports ACTA2 variants identified in Alzheimer's disease patients; the ACTA2 variant literature here (Arg179/Arg258 pathogenic variants) concerns smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, thoracic aortic disease, moyamoya-like cerebral arteriopathy and stroke (PMIDs 22831780, 33199432, 39822761, 28814167), which are cerebrovascular rather than AD phenotypes, so Established is excluded. Supportive but indirect biology exists: ACTA2 marks vascular smooth muscle cells whose phenotype is lost around amyloid-laden vessels in post-mortem human AD brain (PMID 33915754), and medin amyloid, linked to AD and vascular dementia, activates human brain VSMCs (PMID 39345549). A bioinformatics hub-gene analysis of AD and obstructive sleep apnea (PMID 34916831) may list ACTA2 as a co-expression hub, which is expression-level, not variant-level, evidence. Several remaining papers mention ACTA2 only as a smooth muscle marker or in unrelated contexts (PMIDs 39988732, 40195303, 31554736, 9461526), representing incidental co-mention. The weight therefore sits on Hypothesized, with some probability for Existing given that ACTA2-driven cerebral small-vessel/white-matter injury is a recognized risk pathway for dementia.

Every article provided concerns ARL13B as a ciliary small GTPase involved in ciliogenesis, Hedgehog signaling, interneuron migration, photoreceptor outer segment formation, kidney cyst formation, and Joubert syndrome; none report any measurement, association, or mechanistic link to type 2 diabetes, glycemia, insulin secretion, or obesity. The only human genetic evidence (PMIDs 18674751, 25869670, 32639540) links ARL13B variants to Joubert syndrome and related ciliopathies, not to a diabetes precursor phenotype. Ciliary dysfunction is broadly relevant to metabolic syndromes (e.g., Bardet–Biedl), which leaves a small residual possibility of a hypothesized biological link, but no paper here supports it. Therefore the relationship with type 2 diabetes is best classified as Novel, with a minor allowance for Hypothesized based on general cilium–metabolism biology.

Every substantive article on CAPN3 in this list concerns limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A/LGMDR1, calpainopathy, and related inherited myopathies, with no mention of autism spectrum disorder phenotypes or neurodevelopmental outcomes. The only document mentioning autism is a large conference abstract compilation (PMID 27454254) that includes unrelated abstracts on autism awareness and exome sequencing in Saudi families; this is an incidental co-mention within a heterogeneous proceedings volume, not evidence of a CAPN3–ASD relationship. No study reports CAPN3 variants in ASD probands, and the gene's known biology (skeletal muscle-specific calcium-dependent protease, sarcomere maintenance) offers no direct mechanistic link to ASD. Therefore the relationship is best classified as Novel, with a small residual allowance for a hypothesized biological connection.

No article reports variants in CCDC33 associated with or causing type 2 diabetes; there are no probands, families, or association cohorts, so Established and Existing are essentially unsupported. The only diabetes-adjacent paper (PMID 28639886) lists CCDC33 as part of a 32-gene expression classifier distinguishing diabetic from non-diabetic pancreatic cancer patients and places it in a ceRNA network, which is a weak, exploratory transcriptomic co-mention rather than evidence for a role in type 2 diabetes pathogenesis; this gives only marginal support to a Hypothesized relationship. The remaining articles concern CCDC33 biology in motile cilia distal tips (PMID 41423487) and candidate risk genes for nonobstructive azoospermia (PMID 36259570), both unrelated to glucose metabolism or insulin biology. Overall the evidence base is best described as Novel, with some weight to Hypothesized owing to the differential-expression finding in diabetic patients.

One human genetic association study (PMID 22628130) reports a significant association between ADRB2 gene-region variation and early-onset bipolar disorder (OR ~1.8) in 443 patients vs 1,731 controls, though replication failed due to poor genotyping coverage in the WTCCC sample — this constitutes credible but limited, non-definitive evidence consistent with "Existing". An earlier linkage study (PMID 7986886) actually excluded linkage of ADRB2 to bipolar disorder in Amish and Icelandic pedigrees, weakening but not eliminating the association evidence. Supporting biological plausibility includes β2-adrenergic signaling in mood regulation and Adrb2 as an FTO/m6A target in rodent depression-like behavior (PMID 34836959), but that is animal work and relates to depression, supporting only "Hypothesized". Most other listed articles concern asthma, COPD, cardiomyopathy, obesity, or meningitis and are irrelevant homonym/unrelated-phenotype papers. No two independent human studies demonstrate causal variants in bipolar probands or families, so "Established" is essentially excluded.

None of the provided articles report ARL13B variants in autism probands or families; the human genetic evidence concerns Joubert syndrome (PMID 18674751, 23692786), a ciliopathy with psychomotor delay and intellectual disability, which is only indirectly linked to ASD. The strongest autism-relevant evidence is mechanistic and in mouse: conditional Arl13b deletion in interneurons disrupts GABAergic morphology, synaptic connectivity, and excitatory/inhibitory balance (PMID 28787594), and Arl13b is required for radial glial polarity and cortical neuronal placement (PMID 23817546), plus axon guidance of cerebellar tracts (PMID 34132778) — all plausible ASD-relevant neurodevelopmental mechanisms but not direct phenotype evidence in humans. Therefore the bulk of probability falls on Hypothesized, with some weight on Existing if one accepts Joubert syndrome/ciliopathy neurodevelopmental phenotypes as a recognized ASD-associated condition. Established is essentially excluded because no article here demonstrates ARL13B variants causing ASD in independent human probands.

None of the provided ADRB2 articles address epilepsy; they concern asthma/beta-agonist pharmacogenetics (PMIDs 32256100, 24641588, 27091647, 26629374), cardiomyopathy and cardiovascular/sepsis genetics (25979592, 30660782, 39107277), analgesia/labor (23972758, 30281924), and general pharmacogenomics (18855611, 34516287, 26221068). The epilepsy-related papers (15972249, 2574420, 25771138, 26970394, 24321005, 181242, 12782191) are animal seizure models or unrelated mechanisms and never mention ADRB2; some use "bar" (pressure/rota-rod) incidentally rather than the gene. The only indirect CNS link is an animal study showing Adrb2 as an FTO m6A target in depression-like behavior (34836959), which concerns mood, not seizures, and is murine. Thus there is no human genetic association, nor even a clearly articulated biological pathway tying ADRB2 variation to epileptogenesis, leaving the relationship essentially unsupported with only a weak speculative CNS-expression rationale.

No article reports ADRB2 variants causing schizophrenia in independent probands or families, so Established is effectively excluded. The strongest human genetic data (PMID 22212732) links the ADRB2 Gly16 allele to sexual adverse events during risperidone treatment in schizophrenia inpatients — a pharmacogenetic phenotype within schizophrenia patients rather than disease susceptibility, which supports at most a limited "Existing"-type association. PMID 38036718 provides substantial biological rationale: ADRB2 agonists reduce astrocyte phagocytosis (relevant to aberrant synaptic pruning in schizophrenia), pathway analysis links ADRB2 to schizophrenia, and an EHR observational study suggests salmeterol exposure reduced inpatient psychiatric visits — mechanistic/pharmacological, not variant-based. PMID 40530435 identifies ADRB2 as a shared hub gene in schizophrenia–sleep disorder comorbidity via transcriptomics and mouse models, again mechanistic. Remaining articles are incidental co-mentions (asthma, cardiomyopathy, fibromyalgia, sepsis, pharmacogenomics reviews), so the evidence weight falls mainly on Hypothesized with meaningful probability for Existing.

None of the provided articles report C10ORF90 variants in epilepsy patients; the epilepsy-related papers (ketogenic diet, GLUT1-DS, Scn1a mice, mitochondrial disease, Rett syndrome, CPT-1A) do not mention the gene at all and are topically unrelated. C10ORF90 appears only in contexts of 10q26 terminal deletions (multi-gene CNVs listing it as a candidate for intellectual disability, which cannot implicate this gene specifically), tuberculosis resistance GWAS, breast cancer (FATS) polymorphism, centrosome/cilium biology, and an Alzheimer's multi-omics screen. The centrosomal/ciliary function and neural expression in glia provide only a weak, indirect biological rationale that could be stretched toward neurodevelopmental excitability phenotypes, justifying a minority weight on Hypothesized. Overall the gene–epilepsy co-mention is incidental, so Novel is most appropriate.

None of the provided articles address Alzheimer's disease in any way. The CCDC33 findings concern susceptibility to pneumococcal meningitis (PMID: 31092817), motile cilia distal-tip organization in frog/mouse/human multiciliated cells (PMID: 41423487), and candidate risk variants for nonobstructive azoospermia (PMID: 36259570). None of these phenotypes is a recognized precursor, subtype, or mechanistic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, and no expression, pathway, or neurodegeneration-related data are presented. There is therefore no genetic or biological basis in this literature linking CCDC33 to Alzheimer's disease, supporting a "Novel" classification.

No article in this list reports CAPN3 sequence variants associated with or causing type 2 diabetes in human probands or families; all CAPN3 variant studies (PMIDs 27259757, 28881388, 14578192, 23597518, 30919934, 33250842) concern limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A, and the one T2DM co-mention (PMID 25200581) is an incidental comorbidity in an autopsy case. The genetic diabetes link in the reviews (PMIDs 11516996, 12843569, 18193633) consistently points to CAPN10, not CAPN3. The human studies linking CNTF to ASD are all protein/biomarker measurements (elevated or altered serum CNTF levels in children and adults with ASD), not genetic variant association studies (PMID 29869578, 41793951, 40410251, 39588547). No article reports CNTF sequence variants, SNPs, or copy number changes in ASD probands or families; the CNTF polymorphism literature here concerns muscle strength, eating disorders, gambling disorder, and ALS, which are unrelated homolog phenotypes. Supporting mechanistic data come from rodent and in vitro models (CNTF peptide mimetic P6 rescuing autistic-like features in rats; CNTF-driven astrocyte differentiation in FXS iPSC models; Cntf upregulation in a valproic acid rat model), which are strong biological plausibility but not human genetic evidence. Therefore the relationship is best described as Hypothesized, with a modest allowance for "Existing" because repeated human biomarker associations could be argued to constitute limited human evidence of CNTF involvement.

No article in this set reports a genetic variant in CNTF associated with type 2 diabetes in human probands or families; the human genetic studies of CNTF variants (e.g., the G/A null allele, CNTFR C174T) concern muscle strength, fat-free mass, grip strength, and eating-disorder subphenotypes (PMIDs 11247915, 12807897, 16696750, 25637336, 33291384, 20219210), not glycemic traits. The strong CNTF–T2D connection in this literature is biological and pharmacological: CNTF/Axokine and designer gp130 cytokines improve insulin sensitivity, glucose tolerance, and obesity in rodent models and human obesity trials (PMIDs 12861475, 12684362, 31554967, 18210031), plus mechanistic work in rat islets and adipocytes (PMIDs 19272793, 12424252). This supports Hypothesized rather than Established or Existing. A small weight is given to Existing because CNTF/CNTFR variants are linked in humans to body composition and BMI-related traits, which are risk factors loosely connected to T2D, but no direct T2D variant association is demonstrated.

The only available article (PMID: 34009673) describes biallelic truncating CENATAC (CCDC84) mutations causing constitutional mosaic variegated aneuploidy via defective minor (U12-dependent) spliceosome function; autism spectrum disorder is not mentioned or assessed in any patient. No study reports CENATAC variants in ASD probands or families, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. A weak hypothetical basis exists because other minor spliceosome components (e.g., RNU4ATAC) and chromosomal instability are associated with neurodevelopmental phenotypes, but this is indirect and not articulated in the cited literature. Therefore the evidence overwhelmingly supports a Novel classification, with modest weight to Hypothesized based on general minor-spliceosome/neurodevelopment biology.

The only direct human genetic study of CNTF in Alzheimer's disease here (PMID 9342199) explicitly tested the CNTF null allele in 93 AD patients and found no association, and it cites prior reports that this variant does not predispose to AD; the population-genetics survey (PMID 9790747) only notes APOE, not CNTF, as an AD risk locus. Other CNTF variant studies in humans concern muscle strength/sarcopenia, grip strength, eating disorders and gambling disorder (PMIDs 16696750, 25637336, 31861518, 33291384, 20219210, 35484167), phenotypes not established as AD precursors. However, CNTF biology is clearly relevant to neurodegeneration: it is discussed as a candidate neuroprotective/therapeutic cytokine for AD and multiple sclerosis (PMID 26187860), appears in neurotrophin/cytokine reviews of neurodegeneration (PMIDs 9106250, 9700665), and modulates glial/TSPO responses studied alongside AD tissue (PMID 31242048). Thus the evidence supports a biologically hypothesized rather than a genetically established or replicated association, with a small residual probability that an unexamined cohort study (e.g., VITA, PMID 18603262) reported a positive CNTF–AD association.

None of the provided articles report any genetic variant in CHRNA9 associated with Alzheimer's disease in humans; the only AD-related paper (PMID 17610911) concerns amyloid-β and nicotine-enhanced LTP mediated by α7 nAChRs, not α9, so CHRNA9 is not implicated there. The remaining CHRNA9 literature concerns cochlear efferent transmission (PMIDs 19166271, 14757515, 35573302), pain and conotoxin pharmacology (24641230, 26426047, 20368690), immune/inflammatory modulation (23399696, 31817275), cancer (22125646), nicotine dependence (25450229), and Graves' disease (21841780) — none a recognized Alzheimer's precursor or mechanism. The broad relevance of nicotinic cholinergic signaling to AD gives a weak, indirect biological rationale, which could justify a "Hypothesized" reading, but α9-containing receptors are largely non-neuronal/cochlear and no data here link them to amyloid, tau, or cognition in AD. Therefore the co-mentions appear largely incidental, favoring Novel with substantial residual weight on Hypothesized.

All retrieved articles concern CORO1A's role in actin regulation, T-cell egress, severe combined immunodeficiency, EBV-driven lymphoproliferation, and epidermodysplasia verruciformis-like phenotypes (e.g., PMIDs 18836449, 19097825, 23522482, 26476480, 37915722). None of the provided articles examines schizophrenia at all. The DAD1 literature here concerns the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, N-linked glycosylation, and anti-apoptotic function in hamster cells, yeast, and mouse embryos (PMIDs 8413235, 9748289, 9167970, 10748466, 10720432, 7593165), plus human genetic associations with asthma/atopy (PMIDs 30032071, 39615807) — a phenotype unrelated to schizophrenia. The dopamine D1 receptor rat study (PMID 36191805) and the plant "DAD1" (DEFECTIVE IN ANTHER DEHISCENCE1) papers use homonymous acronyms and must be dismissed, including the D1-receptor/motivation link that superficially touches neuropsychiatric amotivation. No human variant, expression, or pathway evidence connects DAD1 to schizophrenia, so the relationship is best described as Novel, with a small allowance for a generic apoptosis/neurodevelopment rationale.

None of the provided articles mention bipolar disorder at all. The CORO1A literature is overwhelmingly about immunology: severe combined immunodeficiency, EBV-associated lymphoproliferation, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, and actin/T-cell biology (PMIDs 18836449, 23522482, 26476480, 37915722). The only neuropsychiatric connections are incidental: CORO1A lies within the recurrent 16p11.2 CNV region associated with autism/ADHD (PMIDs 19097825, 35715439, 38684311), but such multigene deletions cannot implicate CORO1A specifically, and the phenotypes described are not bipolar disorder. One hypothalamus atlas paper links rare CORO1A variants to BMI (PMID 39910307), which is metabolic rather than affective. Therefore the gene–bipolar relationship is essentially unsupported, with only a weak speculative basis via 16p11.2 neurodevelopmental pleiotropy.

The CORO1A literature here is overwhelmingly immunological: biallelic/hemizygous CORO1A variants cause T-cell lymphopenia, atypical SCID, EBV-driven lymphoproliferation and epidermodysplasia verruciformis (PMIDs 23522482, 26476480, 25073507, 34913575, 37915722, 42318436). None of these reports describe epilepsy or seizures as part of the phenotype. The only neurological link is indirect, via the recurrent 16p11.2 CNV that encompasses CORO1A among ~40 genes and is associated with neurodevelopmental disease, autism and ADHD (PMIDs 19097825, 35715439, 38684311); a multigenic CNV cannot single out CORO1A, and epilepsy is not specifically attributed to it. One paper notes CORO1A expression in hypothalamic neurons and a BMI association (PMID 39910307), offering only weak, non-epilepsy brain relevance. Overall the gene–epilepsy relationship appears incidental, with a small residual chance that CNV-based neurodevelopmental/seizure phenotypes could be argued as a hypothesized link.

The only available article (PMID 34009673) reports biallelic truncating CENATAC (CCDC84) mutations in patients with constitutional mosaic variegated aneuploidy and defines CENATAC as a minor spliceosome component; epilepsy or seizures are not mentioned as a phenotype in the results. There is therefore no human genetic evidence linking CENATAC variants to epilepsy, and no replication in independent probands with a seizure phenotype. A weak biological rationale exists because minor spliceosome dysfunction (e.g., RNU4ATAC-related disorders) and chromosomal instability syndromes can involve neurodevelopmental features that sometimes include seizures, which supports a modest allocation to Hypothesized. Overall the evidence best fits Novel, with some probability for Hypothesized.

The CORO1A-specific literature here concerns immunodeficiency phenotypes (SCID, EBV-driven lymphoproliferation, epidermodysplasia verruciformis, Th17/TGFβ signaling) and metabolic/hypothalamic BMI genetics, with no study testing CORO1A variants in schizophrenia patients. The schizophrenia-related articles (demyelination, oligodendrocyte cell-cycle, collagen XIX, RanBP9) do not implicate CORO1A at all and are incidental co-mentions. The only neuropsychiatric touchpoint is the 16p11.2 CNV paper, but that rearrangement spans ~40 genes and cannot single out CORO1A, and its outcome was blood cell counts, not psychosis. Weak biological plausibility exists via CORO1A expression in microglia and neuroinflammatory/lysosomal trafficking roles, which supports a modest Hypothesized weighting, but no credible human genetic association with schizophrenia is presented.

None of the provided articles mention epilepsy or seizures in any context. The DAD1 literature here concerns its role as an oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) subunit and anti-apoptotic factor in hamster cells, yeast (OST2), and knockout mice (embryonic lethality), plus plant homonymous DAD1 (DEFECTIVE IN ANTHER DEHISCENCE1), which is an unrelated gene and should be dismissed. The only human genetic association studies link DAD1/OXA1L variants to asthma and atopy, not epilepsy. A weak indirect mechanistic argument could be made because defects in N-linked glycosylation (congenital disorders of glycosylation) and neuronal apoptosis pathways frequently manifest with seizures, which supports a small allocation to Hypothesized; however, no abstract here makes that connection, so most weight goes to Novel.

The only article linking DAD1 to autism is PMID 39154487, which proposes DAD1 (with ASPG) as a placental-derived biomarker for ASD-like symptom severity in offspring — an expression/biomarker finding ("ASD-like symptoms" suggests a model system), not a genetic variant association in human probands. No study in the list reports DAD1 sequence variants segregating with or associated with ASD in patients, so Established is excluded and Existing is weakly supported at best. The remaining literature concerns DAD1's role in the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, N-linked glycosylation, and apoptosis (PMIDs 8413235, 9748289, 9167970, 10965038), with knockout mouse embryonic lethality and increased apoptosis (PMIDs 10336695, 10720432, 10748466); congenital-disorder-of-glycosylation and apoptosis biology are plausibly relevant to neurodevelopment, supporting a hypothesized relationship. Human genetic association studies for DAD1 exist only for asthma/atopy (PMIDs 30032071, 39615807), an unrelated phenotype, and several hits are the plant DAD1 homonym (jasmonate biosynthesis), which should be dismissed.

The only human link between CORO1A and ASD comes from its position within the recurrent 16p11.2 CNV region: PMID 19097825 describes a girl with a paternal 2-bp CORO1A mutation plus a de novo 600-kb maternal 16p11.2 deletion who had SCID and attention deficit/hyperactivity, with the neurodevelopmental phenotype explicitly attributed to the multigene CNV rather than CORO1A itself; PMID 35715439 similarly treats 16p11.2 CNVs as neurodevelopmentally relevant while studying blood counts. A multigene deletion cannot single out CORO1A, so no paper here demonstrates causality for ASD through CORO1A-specific variants, precluding Established. All other CORO1A reports concern immunodeficiency (SCID, EBV susceptibility, epidermodysplasia verruciformis), hematopoiesis, microglial α-synuclein trafficking, or BMI, with no autism phenotype. The gene is nonetheless brain-expressed and resides in a bona fide ASD risk locus, which supports a weak Existing/Hypothesized position rather than complete novelty.

The only provided article (PMID 34009673) identifies biallelic truncating CENATAC (CCDC84) mutations as a cause of constitutional mosaic variegated aneuploidy, with functional work establishing CENATAC as a minor spliceosome component; schizophrenia is not mentioned or studied anywhere in this literature. There are no genetic association studies, case reports, or family studies linking CENATAC variants to schizophrenia. A tenuous indirect argument could be made that minor spliceosome dysfunction and chromosomal instability affect neurodevelopment, which might support a "Hypothesized" reading, but the paper offers no neural phenotype or psychiatric relevance. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel, with a small residual allowance for a biology-based hypothesis.

No study in this set reports DAD1 genetic variants in Alzheimer's disease patients or families, so Established is excluded; the only human genetic association studies for DAD1 variants concern asthma/atopy (PMIDs 30032071, 39615807), which are not recognized precursors or risk factors for AD. However, there is directly relevant biological evidence: in human brain pericytes, Dutch-mutant Aβ1-40 upregulated DAD1 (defender against cell death-1) mRNA, and DAD1 protein was detected in a subset of senile plaques in AD brains (PMID 15175081), providing an expression/mechanistic link to AD pathology. Supporting biology places DAD1 in apoptosis regulation, N-linked glycosylation, and ER stress responses (PMIDs 8413235, 9748289, 10965038, 27761878), pathways plausibly involved in neurodegeneration, though demonstrated in non-human or in vitro systems. Several retrieved articles are plant DAD1 (DEFECTIVE IN ANTHER DEHISCENCE1) homonyms and were disregarded. Overall the evidence best fits Hypothesized, with residual probability for Novel since the AD link rests on a single expression study.

No human genetic study links DAD1 variants to type 2 diabetes; the only T2D-related article (PMID 23390342) is a mouse transcriptomic/text-mining study identifying Dad1 among a cluster of genes overexpressed in diabetes-resistant C57BL/6J ob/ob versus BTBR ob/ob mice, proposing a role in beta-cell survival and compensation. This provides biologically relevant, non-human, expression-based support consistent with "Hypothesized" rather than "Existing" or "Established." Supporting mechanistic work shows DAD1 is an oligosaccharyltransferase subunit whose loss triggers apoptosis and ER stress (PMIDs 8413235, 9748289, 9167970, 10965038, 27761878), a pathway plausibly relevant to beta-cell failure, though not studied in diabetic humans. The human genetic association studies for DAD1 concern asthma/atopy, not diabetes (PMIDs 30032071, 39615807), and the Arabidopsis DAD1 (DEFECTIVE IN ANTHER DEHISCENCE1) papers are homonym hits that should be dismissed.

No article demonstrates that CORO1A variants cause type 2 diabetes; the CORO1A literature is dominated by immunodeficiency phenotypes (SCID, EBV susceptibility, epidermodysplasia verruciformis), and the CDKN1C/KCNQ1 diabetes papers are unrelated homonym/neighbour-gene content. The strongest relevant human genetic evidence is the HYPOMAP study (PMID 39910307), which reports that rare deleterious CORO1A variants associate with BMI at the population level, a well-recognized risk factor strongly linked to type 2 diabetes — supporting "Existing" but only indirectly for T2D itself. Human expression data showing upregulation of TACO/coronin-1 in PBMCs of type 2 diabetes patients (PMID 26089620) provides biological/expression plausibility, fitting "Hypothesized." The 16p11.2 CNV paper (PMID 35715439) cannot isolate CORO1A and concerns blood counts, not diabetes. Thus the evidence sits between Existing (via BMI variant association) and Hypothesized (via expression in T2D patients), with Established excluded.

There is no human genetic variant evidence, no psychiatric phenotype, and no biological pathway argument linking DDX55 to mood disorders. The gene–phenotype pairing appears entirely incidental, supporting a Novel classification.

The only provided article links CENATAC (CCDC84) biallelic truncating mutations to constitutional mosaic aneuploidy via minor spliceosome dysfunction, with no mention of Alzheimer's disease, neurodegeneration, or cognitive phenotypes. While minor intron splicing defects can broadly affect neuronal genes, this is speculative and not stated in the literature provided. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel.

The only available article links biallelic truncating CENATAC (CCDC84) mutations to constitutional mosaic aneuploidy via defective minor (U12-dependent) spliceosome function and chromosome segregation errors; bipolar disorder is never mentioned. There is no genetic, expression, or pathway evidence connecting CENATAC to bipolar disorder, nor any psychiatric phenotype in the reported patients. While minor spliceosome dysfunction is broadly relevant to neurodevelopment, this is too tenuous and unsupported in the provided literature to justify a Hypothesized rating. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel.

Every provided article concerns DNAI1 in the context of primary ciliary dyskinesia, outer dynein arm defects, laterality/situs anomalies, asthenospermia, or motile cilia biology; none mention Autism Spectrum Disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. A small residual probability is retained for "Hypothesized" because motile/primary cilia biology has been loosely invoked in neurodevelopmental pathways, but no such link is made here. No article reports DAD1 variants in patients with congenital heart disease; there are no probands, families, or association studies for this phenotype. Human genetic association data for DAD1 exist only for asthma/atopy (PMIDs 30032071, 39615807), an unrelated phenotype. The remaining evidence is mechanistic/animal: Dad1-null mice show embryonic lethality, increased apoptosis, and impaired mesodermal development (PMIDs 10336695, 10748466, 10720432, 9121464), plus OST-complex/N-glycosylation function (PMIDs 9748289, 9167970), which provides only a weak, nonspecific developmental rationale rather than any heart-specific link; several plant DAD1 (jasmonate biosynthesis) papers are homonymous and were dismissed. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel, with some weight to Hypothesized based on the apoptosis/embryonic-development animal data.

The only provided article describes CENATAC (CCDC84) as a minor spliceosome component whose biallelic truncating mutations cause constitutional mosaic aneuploidy and chromosome segregation errors. Therefore the evidence base supports a Novel classification, with only a small allowance for hypothesized relevance via general minor-spliceosome roles in metabolic tissues.

No article reports CORO1A variants associated with or causing Alzheimer's disease; the human genetic literature on CORO1A concerns combined immunodeficiency/SCID, EBV susceptibility, and BMI (PMIDs 23522482, 26476480, 37915722, 39910307), which are unrelated to AD. The strongest AD-relevant data are biological: a human post-mortem study quantified coronin-1A as a microglial motility protein in AD and Aβ42-immunized brains (PMID 31703599), though expression was unchanged versus controls, and a mouse SAMP8/Aβ antisense proteomics study found reduced Coro1a carbonylation with improved cognition (PMID 15932783). Additional support for mechanistic plausibility comes from Coro1A regulating microglial trafficking of pathological protein aggregates and lysosomal/inflammasome stress in neurodegeneration, with elevated protein in human PD brain (PMID 39837661). These are expression/functional/animal data rather than variant-level human association, so "Hypothesized" is the best fit, with some residual probability of "Novel" given the null AD result and otherwise incidental co-mentions (e.g., conference abstract PMID 27534393).

The only available article (PMID 34009673) reports biallelic truncating CENATAC (CCDC84) mutations in patients with constitutional mosaic variegated aneuploidy, identifying CENATAC as a minor spliceosome component whose loss causes chromosome segregation errors. Thus there is no article demonstrating CENATAC variants in patients with CHD, so Established is excluded and Existing is only weakly supported by the indirect argument that constitutional aneuploidy is a recognized mechanism/risk factor for congenital heart disease. The strongest justified category is Hypothesized, based on plausible biology (minor intron splicing defects and aneuploidy, both implicated in developmental/cardiac malformations), with substantial residual probability for Novel given the complete absence of cardiac data.

Every retrieved article concerns DNAI1 (dynein axonemal intermediate chain 1) in the context of primary ciliary dyskinesia, Kartagener syndrome, laterality/situs defects, asthenozoospermia, and congenital heart disease. None of the provided articles examine type 2 diabetes or any diabetes-related metabolic phenotype in relation to CHRNA9. Multiple independent human studies report point mutations in DNAJC5 (p.Leu115Arg, p.Leu116del) segregating in unrelated families with autosomal dominant adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Kufs type A), whose core phenotype is progressive myoclonus epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic and myoclonic seizures. Primary evidence with patient variants is provided by Nosková et al. (PMID 21820099), Benitez et al. (PMID 22073189), and Velinov et al. (PMID 22978711, 20 mutation-positive individuals across three families with seizures as a defining feature), with further independent cases (PMID 40688378, 37566176). These are single-nucleotide/codon-level variants, not multigene CNVs, and show segregation, absence in controls, and functional corroboration. Animal/C. elegans models (PMIDs 36282524, 26395859) add mechanistic support but are not needed for the human causal claim.

The strongest primary evidence is the fetal NGS series (PMID 33131162), which reported a biallelic pathogenic DNAI1 variant in a fetus with complex CHD/heterotaxy — a single human proband-level finding. DNAI1 is an established PCD gene, and PCD cohorts repeatedly document heterotaxy and congenital heart disease (PMIDs 17515466, 30166424, 22499950, 26545972), providing a well-recognized mechanistic link (motile/nodal ciliary dysfunction causing laterality defects and CHD), but most of these papers cite DNAI1 as background rather than reporting DNAI1 variants in CHD patients themselves. One case report (PMID 24912412) found only a rare heterozygous DNAI1 SNP inherited from an unaffected mother in an asplenia syndrome neonate whose candidate causal variant was in DNAH5, so it does not establish causality. I cannot cite two independent studies reporting DNAI1 variants causally in CHD probands, so Established is unlikely; the evidence best fits Existing, with residual weight on Hypothesized given the mechanistic/ciliary rationale.

The evidence base is therefore best described as Novel for the DNAJC5–type 2 diabetes relationship.

None of the provided articles mention bipolar disorder or any psychiatric phenotype. The DAD1 literature here concerns its role as an oligosaccharyltransferase subunit and anti-apoptotic factor (PMIDs 8413235, 9167970, 9748289, 10965038), knockout mouse embryonic lethality/apoptosis (10336695, 10748466, 10720432), ER stress (27761878), cancer/hematology expression (16829574, 27086042), and human genetic associations with asthma/atopy (30032071, 39615807) — not bipolar disorder. The only schizophrenia-related article (PMID 15793701) concerns Epsin 4 (CLINT1/enthoprotin) on chromosome 5q33, a distinct gene from EPN3 (Epsin 3, chromosome 17q21), so it provides no genetic evidence for EPN3 and is effectively a homonym/family-name confound. A modest allowance for "Hypothesized" reflects only the generic biology that epsin-family proteins mediate clathrin-dependent endocytosis—a process implicated in synaptic vesicle trafficking and in the Epsin 4 schizophrenia hypothesis—but EPN3 expression is reported as epithelial/parietal-cell restricted and absent from normal brain. No human genetic association study of EPN3 variants with schizophrenia is present, so Established is excluded and Existing is highly unlikely.

All of the genetic evidence presented links DNAJC5 (CSPα) variants (p.Leu115Arg, p.Leu116del, C128Y, in-frame duplications) to autosomal dominant adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis / Kufs disease (PMIDs 21820099, 22073189, 22978711, 22235333, 35462699, 31919451), not to Alzheimer's disease; the dementia in these patients is part of a distinct lysosomal/progressive myoclonus epilepsy syndrome rather than an AD subtype or precursor. The single dementia case report with a DNAJC5 missense variant (PMID 34720963) concerns early-onset vascular dementia with elevated Lp(a), again not AD. Biologically, however, CSPα is a presynaptic co-chaperone whose loss causes synaptic degeneration, SNARE/SNAP-25 depletion, aberrant palmitoylation (PPT1/CLN1 link), and promotes α-synuclein aggregation (PMIDs 26610600, 26659577, 37566176), mechanisms directly relevant to neurodegenerative proteinopathy and synaptic loss in AD; one paper explicitly invokes a role for CSPα in other neurodegenerative diseases with protein aggregation. This supports a "Hypothesized" relationship rather than demonstrated human genetic association with Alzheimer's disease, with residual probability for "Novel" since the co-mentions are largely incidental to AD itself.

None of the provided articles report genetic variants in ERN2 in schizophrenia patients, so Established and Existing are essentially excluded. The genuine ERN2-specific studies (PMIDs 35727638, 31524632, 30973754) show that ERN2 is expressed exclusively in gastrointestinal and respiratory mucosal epithelia, regulating goblet cell maturation and MUC5B/MUC5AC expression — biology with no plausible CNS or schizophrenia relevance. Remaining papers address ER stress/UPR in Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, retinal degeneration, obesity, and pulmonary fibrosis, again via IRE1α. Thus the co-mentions appear incidental (shared "IRE1/UPR" terminology), favoring Novel, with some weight to Hypothesized given the generic UPR-neuropsychiatric pathway link.

No article reports human genetic variants in ERN2 in autism probands or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is essentially unsupported. The only autism-relevant paper (PMID 29430617) is a mouse study showing ER stress/IRE1–XBP1 signaling in prefrontal cortex alters social behavior, but the sensor involved is the ubiquitous IRE1α/ERN1, not the gut/airway-restricted paralogue ERN2/IRE1β. The remaining ERN2-specific papers concern colonic goblet cells, mucus/colitis, cystic fibrosis and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (PMIDs 35727638, 31524632, 30973754, 11238559), none of which relate to neurodevelopment; other papers address IRE1 biology in retina, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's or plant ERN transcription factors (homonym, PMID 17827349). Thus the gene–phenotype link is largely incidental, with at most a weak pathway-level (ER stress/XBP1 in social behavior) rationale that could support a Hypothesized rating.

None of the provided articles report any genetic variant, association study, or clinical cohort linking ERN2 (IRE1β) to bipolar disorder. The only mention of bipolar disorder is an incidental listing in a general review of ER stress in brain damage (PMID 21266235), which concerns the broader UPR/IRE1 pathway rather than ERN2 specifically. All ERN2-specific studies concern gastrointestinal and airway epithelium — goblet cell development, colitis susceptibility in knockout mice, and mucin regulation in cystic fibrosis and IPF (PMIDs 35727638, 11238559, 31524632, 30973754) — tissues and phenotypes unrelated to bipolar disorder; indeed ERN2 expression is largely restricted to mucosal epithelia, not brain. Remaining papers describe IRE1α (ERN1) biology in metabolism, virology, and retinal degeneration, which are homologous-pathway co-mentions rather than evidence for ERN2 in psychiatric disease. A small amount of probability is retained for "Hypothesized" because a generic ER-stress/UPR rationale for mood disorders is occasionally invoked, but it is not ERN2-specific.

No article reports ESR2 variants in epilepsy patients, families, or probands, so Established and Existing are unsupported. The only epilepsy-relevant evidence is the rat study (PMID 30744972) showing Esr2 expression in parvalbumin-positive cortical interneurons and estradiol-dependent modulation of fast-spiking interneuron excitability across the estrus cycle, explicitly framed around cyclical (catamenial) epilepsy — a plausible biological mechanism for seizure susceptibility, but in animals, not human genetics. Other papers concern ESR2 in dementia, depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, anorexia, fertility, and metabolism, which are co-mentions irrelevant to epilepsy causation. This pattern — a mechanistic/animal link to cortical inhibition without human variant data — fits Hypothesized, with some residual probability of Novel given how thin the epilepsy connection is.

Human candidate-gene association studies report nominal associations of ESR2 SNPs with autistic traits/Asperger syndrome (PMID 19598235) and with symptom severity in ASD (PMID 29526366), and a Chinese Han study found ESR2 promoter hypermethylation correlating with autism severity (PMID 28299627). These are small, nominal, non-genome-wide findings without robust independent replication of specific variants, so they fall short of "Established"—no paper here demonstrates a causal variant in multiple independent probands or families. Supporting biology (ERβ in maternal immune activation models, ERβ agonist rescuing social deficits, VPA rodent models) is animal/mechanistic and only bolsters the "Hypothesized" tier (PMIDs 34531723, 29430617, 40457879). Several listed articles concern unrelated phenotypes (dementia, mammographic density, cattle fertility, colorectal cancer) or unrelated genes (ErbB/NRG3) and do not contribute. Overall the evidence best fits "Existing," with meaningful residual probability for "Hypothesized."

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder in any form; all concern DNAJC5/CSPα in adult neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Kufs disease/CLN4), Parkinsonism, tau/α-synuclein secretion, and lysosomal/chaperone biology. There are no human genetic studies linking DNAJC5 variants to ASD, so Established and Existing are unsupported. A small weight is given to Hypothesized because DNAJC5 is a presynaptic co-chaperone regulating SNARE assembly, synaptic vesicle cycling, and synapse maintenance—pathways broadly implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders—so a biological rationale could be argued indirectly. However, the literature here only co-mentions neurodegeneration, not autism, making Novel the most probable classification.

ERN2 encodes IRE1β, an epithelial-restricted paralogue expressed in gastrointestinal and respiratory mucosa; the papers that specifically study ERN2 concern colonic goblet cell/mucus biology (PMID 35727638), cystic fibrosis airway mucin secretion (PMID 31524632), and MUC5B regulation in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (PMID 30973754), with no neural or Alzheimer-related data. All Alzheimer-relevant "IRE1" literature here (PMIDs 10587643, 28341998, 11146108, 15234121) concerns IRE1α/ERN1, a different gene, including the mouse brain cloning and PS1-mutation UPR studies. No article reports ERN2 variants in AD patients or even ERN2 expression/function in brain, so neither Established nor Existing can be supported. A small amount of probability is kept for Hypothesized because of the general UPR/IRE1 pathway relevance to AD pathogenesis, which could be loosely extended to the paralogue, but the gene–phenotype co-mention is essentially incidental.

Multiple human case-control studies report associations between ESR2 polymorphisms and AD risk or age at onset, including Finnish women (PMID 15944651), women with Down syndrome (PMID 22156442), a multiethnic female cohort (PMID 24326520), and a meta-analysis finding rs4986938 associated with dementia in Asians (PMID 32335869), plus cognitive-performance associations (PMID 27629499). However, several well-powered studies and a drug-target Mendelian randomisation analysis found no association (PMIDs 21673408, 41773198), and the meta-analysis overall was null, so the evidence is associative, inconsistent, and far from demonstrating causation. No study identifies causal ESR2 variants segregating in independent probands or families, which precludes "Established." Supporting biology (ERβ expression in brain, estrogen neuroprotection; PMIDs 34657250, 18288931) reinforces plausibility but is secondary to the human genetic association data, making "Existing" the best fit.

The only primary human genetic study of ESR2 in schizophrenia in this set (PMID 18164902) tested 14 ESR2 SNPs in 585 cases/615 controls and reported no association, so there is no positive replicated variant-level evidence and certainly nothing causal. A narrative review (PMID 41737726) asserts that ERβ/GPER1 signaling and "genetic variation in ESR2 and CYP19A1" are relevant to treatment-resistant schizophrenia, but this is background citation plus mechanistic/pharmacological reasoning (raloxifene adjunctive therapy), not independent genetic data. Strong biological rationale exists—ERβ is the predominant brain estrogen receptor, estrogen modulates dopaminergic/glutamatergic and synaptic plasticity pathways implicated in schizophrenia (PMIDs 28527569, 37193881)—supporting a Hypothesized classification. ESR2 variants have been associated with other neuropsychiatric phenotypes (dementia, depression, anxiety, anorexia; PMIDs 32335869, 22901010, 21570196, 23999524), which provides only indirect support, as these are not recognized schizophrenia precursors. The many NRG1/ErbB4 papers are irrelevant co-mentions of schizophrenia biology, not ESR2.

None of the provided articles mention autism spectrum disorder or any neurodevelopmental phenotype. All retrieved literature concerns EPN3 (Epsin 3) as an endocytic adaptor with oncogenic roles in breast, lung, prostate cancer and glioma, plus epithelial gene-expression network analyses (PMIDs 24940735, 27926932, 39048677, 37186036, 39146303, 30226603, 27765924). No human genetic variant studies, no expression or pathway data linking EPN3 to ASD-relevant neurobiology, and no animal models of ASD are presented. The co-mention of EPN3 and ASD is therefore incidental, supporting a "Novel" classification; a small residual probability is retained for possible plausible biology (clathrin-mediated endocytosis/synaptic vesicle trafficking) not documented in these abstracts.

The only direct genetic study of ESR2 in bipolar disorder (PMID 11807414) was explicitly negative, finding no transmission distortion of the ESR2 3'UTR A1730G variant in 102 Irish bipolar trios, so no human variant-level evidence supports association. However, there is substantial biological rationale: ER-β is highly expressed in brain, estrogen modulates monoaminergic neurotransmission, and a recent framework paper proposes ER-β/GPER1 engagement as a therapeutic mechanism in treatment-resistant male bipolar disorder (PMID 40995073). Additional human studies link ESR2 variants to related but distinct psychiatric phenotypes (depression, anxiety, dementia/AD), which supports plausibility rather than bipolar-specific association (PMIDs 22901010, 21570196, 24326520, 32335869). No article reports causal ESR2 variants in bipolar probands or families, so Established is excluded and Existing is weakly supported at best. Hypothesized therefore best captures the state of the evidence, with a residual possibility of Novel given the negative primary study.

The only articles addressing congenital heart disease concern ERBB2 (PMIDs 27357797, 40329538), a different gene that appears here through acronym confusion with ESR2; these must be dismissed. All genuine ESR2 papers concern reproductive endocrinology, ovarian response, hypospadias, PCOS, anorexia, Alzheimer's, hepatocellular carcinoma, and adult cardiovascular risk markers — none report cardiac malformations or structural heart defects. The closest cardiovascular link is an ESR2 polymorphism associated with fibrinogen levels in postmenopausal women (PMID 22906475), which pertains to acquired adult CVD risk, not congenital heart disease, and general estrogen receptor biology (PMID 28527569) offers only a very indirect, non-cardiac developmental rationale. There is no human variant evidence, no animal cardiac developmental model, and no mechanistic pathway tying ESR2 to cardiac morphogenesis in this corpus, so the relationship is essentially unsupported.

Only one article in the list links FMNL1 to ASD: a human integrative Mendelian randomization/TWAS/colocalization study using eQTL and pQTL data (PMID 39038939), which reports a significant protective causal association of FMNL1 protein levels with ASD and replication in proteome-wide MR. This is credible human genetic evidence of association but is a single study based on instrumented expression/protein levels rather than variants identified in probands or families, so it falls short of "Established" (no two independent clinical studies with patient variants can be cited). All other papers concern FMNL1 cell biology—actin assembly, podosomes, lipid droplets, T-cell migration, immune synapse traffic, leukemia—with no ASD relevance, providing at best generic neuro-irrelevant functional background. Thus "Existing" is most likely, with residual weight on "Hypothesized" should the MR finding be viewed as indirect/non-variant-level evidence.

All provided articles concern DNAJC5/CSPα in adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Kufs disease, CLN4), Parkinsonism, synaptic chaperone biology and protein palmitoylation; none report bipolar disorder phenotypes, cohorts, or association studies. Presynaptic chaperone/SNARE and synaptic proteostasis functions (PMIDs 25800794, 28579939) provide only a weak, generic biological rationale for psychiatric illness, insufficient for a "Hypothesized" designation beyond a small probability. No human genetic variant evidence linking DNAJC5 to bipolar disorder exists in this literature set, so Established and Existing are effectively excluded.

All provided articles concern EPN3 (Epsin 3) in cancer biology — epithelial phenotype networks, breast cancer metastasis, lung adenocarcinoma/NSCLC progression, glioma invasion, prostate cancer metastasis, and miR-145 targeting. The only brain-related paper (glioma, PMID 30226603) concerns tumor invasion via EMT, which provides no mechanistic basis for epileptogenesis. There is therefore no evidence, genetic or biological, linking EPN3 to epilepsy, making "Novel" the appropriate classification.

None of the supplied articles mention schizophrenia; all concern DNAJC5/CSPα in autosomal dominant adult-onset neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Kufs disease), parkinsonism, tau/α-synuclein release, and synaptic proteostasis. A modest weight is given to Hypothesized because CSPα is a presynaptic co-chaperone that maintains SNAP-25 conformation and SNARE complex assembly, and because ANCL patients can present with behavioral/psychiatric symptoms preceding seizures and dementia — biology plausibly relevant to schizophrenia-related synaptic hypotheses (PMIDs 25800794, 28579939, 26610600, 32783189). However, these links are indirect and not phenotype-specific, so the bulk of probability falls on Novel.

Every article provided links DNAJC5 (CSPα) to neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Kufs/adult-onset NCL), parkinsonism, and synaptic proteostasis in neurons; none addresses cardiac development or congenital heart disease. Accordingly, the gene–phenotype relationship for DNAJC5 and congenital heart disease is best classified as Novel.

There are no human genetic studies reporting ERN2 variants associated with T2D or any recognized precursor, excluding Established and largely excluding Existing. Some weight remains for Hypothesized because ERN2 belongs to the same UPR sensor family whose signaling (XBP1 splicing, ER stress) is mechanistically tied to insulin resistance and β-cell failure, providing a plausible but indirect biological rationale.

None of the provided articles mention bipolar disorder or any neuropsychiatric phenotype; all concern EPN3 in cancer biology (breast, lung, glioma, prostate) and epithelial endocytosis/EMT pathways.
